description.summary: A fearsome critter from American lumberjack folklore that always hides behind the nearest object, making it impossible to observe directly; used to explain unexplained disappearances of loggers in the deep woods.
description.full: The hidebehind is a creature from the 'fearsome critters' tradition of late-19th- and early-20th-century North American lumber camps. By definition impossible to see — the moment a person turns to look, the hidebehind darts behind the nearest tree, stump, or stone — it serves both as occupational humour and as a mock-folkloric explanation for loggers who walked into the woods alone and never came back. According to the published tales, the creature is nocturnal, preys on lumberjacks, subsists chiefly on the intestines of its victims, and has a strong aversion to alcohol, which is therefore considered an effective repellent. The story is documented most prominently in Henry H. Tryon's 1939 collection Fearsome Critters and in Walker D. Wyman's 1978 Mythical Creatures of the USA and Canada. The hidebehind belongs to a broader corpus of fearsome critters — including the agropelter, hodag, hugag, hoopsnake, splintercat, squonk, sidehill gouger, and wampus cat — invented or elaborated in lumber camps as initiation pranks for greenhorns and as set-pieces of campfire storytelling.

etymology.origin: American English, lumberjack camp slang of the late 19th to early 20th century, from the creature's defining behaviour of hiding behind objects.
etymology.meaning: Literal compound: a thing that hides behind.
etymology.first_use: Documented in lumberjack tall-tale traditions; appears in Henry H. Tryon's Fearsome Critters (1939).

coloration: unspecified, said to be invisible to direct observation

features.description: Always positions itself behind the nearest tree, stump, rock, or other object; vanishes from view the instant a witness turns toward it
Operates by night and is described as a stalker of solitary loggers
According to Tryon, alcohol is a sufficient repellent — a self-deprecating joke about lumberjack drinking habits

physical.morphology: Never described in detail because, by the rules of the tale, it cannot be observed. Some accounts describe a tall, gaunt, hairy biped; others leave the form unstated.

abilities.description: Moves to remain behind any nearby object faster than the witness can turn
Stalks lone lumberjacks and ambushes them, dragging them away to its lair
Said to eat chiefly the intestines of its victims

behavior.diet: Reportedly carnivorous, with a particular fondness for the intestines of human victims (per Tryon, 1939).
patterns: Targets solitary individuals away from camp
Said to be deterred by alcohol on the breath of intended victims

range.description: Reported throughout the lumber-camp belt of North America: the upper Midwest (Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota), the Pacific Northwest, New England, and adjacent parts of Canada.

first_recorded.source: Lumberjack oral tradition; first published collections in the early 20th century

peak_activity_periods.description: Heyday of large North American lumber camps and of the fearsome-critter tradition

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Stories cluster around the winter logging season, when crews lived in remote camps and exchanged tall tales around the stove.

origins.cultural_roots: Occupational folklore of North American lumber camps in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, drawing on Old World 'wild man' and forest-spirit traditions transplanted into the new logging frontier.
origins.earliest_accounts: Earliest accounts are oral and undated, embedded in lumber-camp storytelling traditions. The earliest sustained written treatment is Henry H. Tryon's Fearsome Critters (Idlewild Press, 1939).
origins.folklore_connections: Part of the 'fearsome critters' corpus alongside the hodag, hugag, agropelter, splintercat, squonk, sidehill gouger, hoopsnake, and wampus cat.

timeline.event: Henry H. Tryon publishes Fearsome Critters (Idlewild Press, Cornwall, NY), with an entry on the hidebehind
timeline.significance: Establishes the modern canonical description of the creature

timeline.event: Walker D. Wyman publishes Mythical Creatures of the USA and Canada (University of Wisconsin – River Falls Press)
timeline.significance: Reintroduces the hidebehind to mid-20th-century academic folklore study

history.modern_era: The hidebehind survives today primarily as a folklore curiosity in regional storytelling, internet-age cryptid lists, and tabletop games. It has no contemporary cryptozoological investigation tradition; folklorists treat it as a tall-tale figure rather than a candidate biological species.

documentary.name: Tryon (1939) Fearsome Critters entry
documentary.description: Print description of the hidebehind in Henry H. Tryon's Fearsome Critters, including its hiding behaviour, predation on lumberjacks, and aversion to alcohol.
documentary.analysis: A literary record of an oral tall-tale tradition, not an evidentiary claim about a biological creature.

skeptical.name: Tall-tale and occupational folklore
skeptical.description: The hidebehind is a humorous occupational legend invented and elaborated in lumber camps to entertain workers, haze new recruits, and provide a mock explanation for genuine workplace deaths in the dangerous logging trade.
evidence_cited: Embedment of the hidebehind in the larger fearsome-critter corpus
The defining 'cannot be seen' rule, which is a literary joke rather than a description of a creature

stories: Tryon's account of the hidebehind devouring lone lumberjacks (1939)
Camp anecdotes of greenhorns sent to spot a hidebehind as a hazing prank
folklore.beliefs: Treated as humorous folklore rather than a sincere belief; the comedic premise is precisely that the creature's existence can never be confirmed.

literature: Mythical Creatures of the USA and Canada — Walker D. Wyman (1978)
other: Recurring entry in modern cryptid bestiaries and online folklore compilations

researchers.name: Henry H. Tryon
researchers.contribution: Compiled Fearsome Critters (1939), the canonical printed source for the hidebehind

researchers.name: Walker D. Wyman
researchers.contribution: Folklorist who collected and republished hidebehind tales in Mythical Creatures of the USA and Canada (1978)
